newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition marches through Belgrade.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition marches through Belgrade.

text.p: Thousands of Serbian opposition supporters took to the streets on Thursday to demand authorities recognise the results of local elections in the biggest demonstrations to hit the capital for three years.
More protests were expected throughout the country on Friday.
Some 20,000 people marched through the capital Belgrade, waving opposition party flags and flinging insults at President Slobodan Milosevic and the ruling Socialists.
It was the fourth day of protests in Belgrade and other towns since the opposition claimed victory in run-off municipal elections held on Sunday. The opposition promised more to come.

Zoran Djindjic, one of three opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition leaders, charged authorities were committing extensive fraud to overturn the vote and said demonstrations would continue until the Socialists verified poll results.
"We will protest every day until we secure this right," Djindjic told independent Belgrade radio B-92.
Tension rose when the crowd at one point gathered in front of the state television station, Milosevic's main propaganda tool, taunting a cordon of policemen.
For a tense half hour, the protesters threw mud, stones, firecrackers and abuse at the policemen before the organizers persuaded them to move on.
The police, brought in by hundreds in riot gear into the capital were visible only in front of state television.
Opposition leaders heading the procession, urged the crowd to remain calm.
"Now we have to show endurance and wisdom. That is what leads towards the victory," Djindjic said.
Electoral officials on Tuesday confirmed the opposition victory in Belgrade, a stunning blow for Milosevic.
But they failed to announce final results in other towns where Zajedno said it also scored clear majorities.
Electoral commissions controlled by the Socialists cited unspecified irregularities in municipalities where the opposition said it won, and ordered another round of voting.
Earlier, opposition leaders inside parliament were unable to speak to the crowd because police allegedly seized sound equipment.
Organisers had to lower string from the fifth floor window and pull up a megaphone so their leaders could be heard.
"They have our sound equipment but we have Belgrade!" Djindjic said, prompting a roar from the crowd.

"We are demanding that authorities recognise the electoral will of the citizens," said Djindjic, expected to take over as mayor of Belgrade. He said a "new era of democracy" had arrived which the authorities could not ignore.

The Socialist party responded for the first time on Thursday. Spokesman Ivica Dacic said the Zajedno coalition prematurely declared it won in several towns and said results would be announced at the end of the "electoral procedure".
He also accused the wife of opposition leader Vuk Draskovic of inciting violence and terrorism in comments to reporters.
Draskovic said his wife was missing and, in what he said was a message to Milosevic, swore to personally "gouge the eyes out" of anyone who harms her.
"This afternoon Milosevic's criminals kidnapped my wife. Nobody knows where is she now," he told Reuters Television.
Serbian police denied they had arrested Danica Draskovic and it was impossible to independently verify the allegations.
State television and radio repeatedly broadcast comments Danica Draskovic made to reporters on Wednesday evening.
Asked if "terrorist" groups should be formed, she had replied: "I can't wait for this to happen."
State television used her statement to corroborate its portrayal of the opposition movement as bent on resorting to violence ahead of run-off elections on November 27.

Demonstrations were also going on in the southern towns of Nis and Pancevo and more protests were planned elsewhere on Friday, when the opposition expected electoral commissions and courts to rule on the poll results.
